newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian market not expecting October rate cut.
newsitem.headline: Australian market not expecting October rate cut.

text.p: Australian markets began a nervous vigil ahead of Tuesday's policy-setting Reserve Bank of Australia (RBA) board meeting, with most economists saying the chances for an immediate interest-rate cut were slim.
Moderating inflation, slowing activity, a stalled labour market and a reduction in government spending -- the conditions for another rate cut are either already met or soon should be.
But while a cut would please the market, most economists believe it will follow the November board meeting.
"There has to be some chance, but I would put it as relatively small, say 10 to 15 percent," Bankers Trust chief economist Chris Caton said of a rate cut occurring this week.
"We think that they will wait until they have another quarter of comfortable inflation data behind them," he said.
Speculation of a rate cut before the end of 1996 has remained strong since July 31, when the RBA cut rates by 0.5 percentage point to 7.0 percent, the first cut in three years.

Of 32 economists surveyed by Reuters on Friday, 23 saw the next move in rates as downward. Only four economists forecast the next move in rates as a rise, while the remainder saw the outlook as unclear or were undecided.
While a rate reduction was the market's favoured option, only two economists expected to see one occur in October, while a further eight said it was a distinct possibility.
Fixed interest markets have aggressively factored in a cut, with December 90-day bank bill futures closing on Monday at a yield of 6.59 percent, 41 points below the official cash rate.

"Given that we're going to have low inflation...at least over the next six to nine months, and activity is pretty slow, I think there's room there for another easing," said Societe Generale chief economist John Edwards.

Those favouring an October cut, such as Edwards, saw it as more likely to happen at the end of the month, after the release of September employment data on October 10, and third-quarter inflation and wages data on October 23 and 24 respectively.
As such the RBA board would give Ian Macfarlane, in his first meeting as Governor, the go-ahead to cut rates in late October provided the data supported it, economists said.
Helping the case for a rate cut was the performance of the Australian dollar since the July 31 rate cut, when many in the foreign exchange market were caught by surprise.
The dollar was heavily sold at the time, but has since recovered to trade around US$0.7900. If the dollar had continued to weaken, another cut could have been prevented by inflation fears.
"The stability of the Australian dollar around US$0.7900 has no doubt strengthened the case for another rate cut," Macqaurie Bank economists said in a commentary.
"However, we think the RBA is more likely to wait for September quarter inflation and wages data before cutting rates," they said.
While the dollar had handled the last cut reasonably well, economists said a further cut would place it under pressure.

"If anything it's probably bad news for the Australian dollar," AMP Investments chief economist Shane Oliver said, because it would narrow the attractive margin for investors between Australian and Japanese interest rates.
"Obviously if you start cutting rates in Australia, then that relative interest differential narrows, and consequently the Australian dollar will become less attractive," he said.
